name: Cloudflare Tunnel
summary: A small daemon, `cloudflared`, dials out from your network to Cloudflare, so servers can be published or reached privately with no public IP and no open inbound ports.
intro: You run `cloudflared` next to your services. It opens four long-lived, outbound connections to at least two Cloudflare data centers, on port 7844 over QUIC or HTTP/2, and keeps them open. Requests then travel back down those connections, so the firewall can block all inbound traffic. A tunnel is a record in your account with a UUID; each running `cloudflared` is a connector, and you can run up to 25 replicas of one tunnel on different hosts for redundancy, with traffic going to the nearest one.

Routes decide what uses the tunnel. A published application maps a public hostname such as `app.example.com` to a local service like `http://localhost:8080` through a CNAME to `<UUID>.cfargotunnel.com`, and gets Cloudflare’s cache, WAF and DDoS protection on the way. A private network route sends traffic from enrolled devices to private IPs or hostnames behind the tunnel, as a VPN replacement, and Workers can reach private services through it too. Besides HTTP, it carries TCP, SSH, RDP and SMB, though for those users also run `cloudflared` on their side. Who may connect is decided separately, usually by Cloudflare Access. Tunnel is available on all plans at no charge.
strengths: No public IP, open port or firewall exception: the origin only makes outbound connections, so it can’t be reached around Cloudflare
Free on all plans, and quick to start: `cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:8080` gives a temporary `trycloudflare.com` address with no account
Up to 25 replicas per tunnel for redundancy, and tunnels can be endpoints in Cloudflare Load Balancing pools for health-checked failover
One connector serves public hostnames, private network routes and Workers VPC at once
limits: Ties your ingress to Cloudflare: if a tunnel stops, its DNS records stay and visitors get a 1016 error
Replicas of one tunnel act as a single endpoint to a load balancer; for steering or session affinity across hosts you need separate tunnels
Non-HTTP services (TCP, SSH, RDP) need client-side software, and quick tunnels are capped at 200 in-flight requests with no uptime guarantee
Accounts are limited to 1,000 tunnels and 1,000 routes, and Free, Pro and Business terms restrict serving video and other large files through proxied hostnames

story: Cloudflare has always worked as a reverse proxy: a site changes its nameservers, and requests reach Cloudflare before the origin. But if an attacker finds the origin’s IP address, they can go around Cloudflare. The usual fix was a GRE tunnel, which Cloudflare called expensive and slow: it needed network teams on both sides, was mostly sold to large companies, and its encapsulation forced a smaller MTU or packet fragmentation.

During its beta the product was called Warp. On April 5, 2018, Dani Grant announced it as Argo Tunnel: a daemon, `cloudflared`, that dials out to Cloudflare, so “for the rest of the internet, it’s unroutable, as if the server is not even there.” It was bundled with the paid Argo Smart Routing, because visitor traffic had to reach the data centers closest to the origin. The same year, the launch of Cloudflare Access suggested pairing the two so an internal app needs no public IP at all.

On April 15, 2021, Cloudflare made the outbound-only connection free for every organization and renamed the product Cloudflare Tunnel. Named Tunnels gave each tunnel a permanent UUID so restarts reconnect instead of creating a new tunnel, and moving to Cloudflare’s Unimog edge load balancer raised the average life of a tunnel connection from minutes to days.

choices.why: Most firewalls already allow outbound traffic, so `cloudflared` needs no inbound rule, and the origin can then refuse everything that does not come through the tunnel.

choices.choice: Bundle it with Argo at first
choices.why: Tunnel traffic had to reach the Cloudflare data centers nearest the origin, which is what Argo Smart Routing did, so Cloudflare included Tunnel with Argo at no extra cost.
Cloudflare wanted Zero Trust security “accessible to everyone, regardless of size, scale, or resources”, and Tunnel was the piece that connects resources to it.

timeline.text: The `cloudflared` repository is created on GitHub
Launched on April 5 as Argo Tunnel, after a beta under the name Warp
Free for everyone and renamed Cloudflare Tunnel on April 15; Named Tunnels get permanent UUIDs
Load Balancing can reach private IPs through tunnels
